role: Director, Nevada Outdoor Recreation Association, Inc.
summary: Charles S. Watson, Jr., representing the Nevada Outdoor Recreation Association, strongly opposes uncontrolled ORV use on public lands, citing severe ecological damage to the fragile Great Basin desert environment, including toxic plant infestations and lasting soil disturbance. He criticizes the draft EIS for failing to address BLM range conversion projects as a related environmental issue, and proposes a system of designated 'Adventure Roads' to channel ORV use while protecting roadless areas. He also objects strenuously to what he views as politically motivated, environmentally insensitive commentary from officials like Governor O'Callaghan, urging that public land policy prioritize genuine environmental stewardship over narrow utilitarian interests.

statement.text:
TESTIMONY STATEMENT
Subject: Draft Environmental Impact Statement by USDI affecting Off-Road Vehicular uses on the public lands
On February 8, 1972, President Richard M. Nixon issued Executive Order #11644, which directed the U.S. Department of Interior to develop a unified interagency policy for the purpose of alleviating the growing use of off-road vehicles(ORV) on essentially defacto roadless public lands. In his executive order, the president apparently recognizes the massive debilitating effects of ORV use and that such use has become a major threat to our desert environment.
The Nevada Outdoor Recreation Association, Inc. has long expressed its grave concern over ORV activities on the public lands, and has attempted to develop meaningful solutions which would allow for reasonable ORV use on the public lands while restricting such use where there are fragile flora, wildlife, unique-natural, wilderness, archeological, historic, recreational and open space values.
In 1967, this organization began consulting the St.Louisbased Committee For Environmental Information(CEI), one of
the nation's foremost and widely respected environmental\ninstitutions, which includes amongst its trustees the noted\necologist, Dr. Barry Commoner. Our consultations with CEI
were mainly co-ordinated through its science director, Dr.

Kevin P. Shea. Basically, recent investigations by CEI has developed information which tends to conclude that our Great Basin desert and steppe environment is one of the most fragile and most threatened in North America. The threat posed takes many forms and one of the most serious is toxic, poisonous, exotic and nonpalatable plant infestations due to man-made disturbance of both the soil and plant communities. Since 1942, when the notorious poisonous Ukrainian plant halogeton was first detected near Wells, Nevada, this and several other strains of toxic and poisonous exotic plants have taken over an estimated 20,000,000 acres of western rangelends. Almost all of this biological destructionknown to ecologists as an "eco-catastrophe"—can be directly traced to man-made effects, such as roads, railroad beds, pipelines, transmission lines and worst of all—Bureau of Land Management range conversion projects. The latter has been described by these reputable ecologists at CEI, and other respected organizations, as the most destructive program ever fostered by the Federal government on our western rangelands. Make no mistake about it, the chief objection this organization has with this MEPA impact statement is its failure to recognize range conversion as a lagitimate issue in these proceedings.
As we see it, there is little to choose between the debilitating effects of programs that call for massive removal of native plants and plantings of notoriously undependable enotic grasses—the sole objective of which is to convert huge acreages of public lands over to one <u>dominant use</u> for the livestock industry—and these which fail to control the enormous harm now being wrought by indiscriminate ORV use on the public lands. Recently, the National Wildlife Federation—the nation's largest conservation organisation—cited ORV use as the chief cause of massive destructive effects

in the Mojave Desert and along the Colorado River. To paraphrase National Wildlife, ORV use in the Mojave Desert is rapidly converting that once magnificent desert region into one vast slum.
One source of vivid, irrefutable evidence of vehicular use destruction can still be seen in many of the early pioneer emigrant trails which crisscrossed the Creat Basin during the early and mid-1800's. The Oregon Trail, for instance, has not seen use since its abandonment in 1872—yet, in many areas the trail ruts are still there, with their complement of exotic infesting plants, a century after vehicular use(in this instance, by covered wagons) ceased. The same destructive effects can be directly attributed to ORV use on defacto roadless public lands. One far-reaching form of remedial action proposed by NORA has been the selective designation of existing remote and back country primitive, jeep and macadam roads and trails (excluding, in the latter case, those lands deemed suitable for wilderness and natural area preservation) as part of a system of Adventure Roads. Since 1958, when NORA began its pioneer effort to seek out and identify scenic, unique-natural, wilderness, and recreational sites and arcss (which now numbers mearly 450 in Nevada alone), we have included in our program a comprehensive inventory of roads and trails which would be cuitable for this Adventure Roads program on our public lands. Where we observed such roads and trails in exceptional open space conditions, we included—and are presently still developing—a district by district plan for open space receives. The latter would include a system of 24 Adventure Roads, while restricting use of ORV's over defecto roadless

to a continuing inventory and analysis to determine the existence of fragile scenic, unique-hatural and wilderness conditions as well as attempts to identify endangered species habitats and valuable forage areas needing further ORV restrictions.
Lastly, may we further inject our strenuous objections to those who would use these proceedings to promote purely transient utilitarian criteria while demonstrating almost total insensitivity to paramount environmental considerations. What these proceedings need the least are gratuitous, self-serving political rhetoric on the part of certain politicians-whose sole concerns are for the predatory vested interests who are the root cause of this malignant public land environmental crisis. Specifically, we object-most strenuously—to the naive, irrelevant remarks attributed to Governor Mike O'Callaghan in the Nevada press last July 3 and 4. We are sorely distressed over what appears to be a complete changeover from the environmental concern he registered during the governor's early days in office. We consider it appropriate to advise the governor—as it pertains to the issues in these proceedings—to spend more time doing his "homework" on them. In short, the mark that distinguishes a politician from a statesman might be described as the ability to put brain in gear before accelerating one's mouth. We sincerely hope that Hevada political leaders, in addressing this gravely serious problem, will focus their concern on what constitutes the public interest. Indeed, there must be an over-riding awareness that our public lands constitute a priceless 21 stional treasure and heritage—which must be protected and managed in the best interests of all Americans.
Respectfully submitted.
Charles S. Watson.Jr.
Director
